'''David Ritz Finkelstein''' (July 19, 1929 – January 24, 2016) was an emeritus professor of [[physics]] at the [[Georgia Institute of Technology]].<ref name="Cvitanovic2017">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Cvitanović
 | first1 = Predrag
 | last2 = Susskind
 | first2 = Leonard
 | title = David Ritz Finkelstein
 | journal = Physics Today
 | volume = 70
 | issue = 2
 | pages = 68–69
 | year = 2017
 | doi = 10.1063/pt.3.3472
| bibcode = 2017PhT....70b..68C
 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref><ref name="Bio">{{cite web
 |url = https://www.davidritzfinkelstein.com/biography.html
 |title = David Ritz Finkelstein (July 19, 1929 - January 24, 2016) Biography
 |author = Aria Ritz Finkelstein
 |date = 2022
 |website = davidritzfinkelstein.com
 |access-date = 2022-03-11
}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Born in [[New York City]], Finkelstein obtained his Ph.D. in physics at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1953 and taught at [[Stevens Institute of Technology]] through 1960, while he also held a Ford Foundation Fellowship at the [[CERN|European Organization for Nuclear Research]] from 1959 to 1960.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.physics.gatech.edu/user/david-finkelstein|title=David Finkelstein's homepage|last=|first=|date=|website=|publisher=Georgia Tech|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110913092637/https://www.physics.gatech.edu/user/david-finkelstein|archive-date=13 September 2011|access-date=12 June 2015}}</ref> From 1964 to 1976, he was professor of physics at [[Yeshiva University]]. He became a member of the faculty at Georgia Tech in 1980.

David Finkelstein was the first, in 1958, who identified [[Schwarzschild metric|Schwarzschild's solution]] of the [[Einstein field equations]] as corresponding to a region in space from which nothing escapes.<ref name="Finkelstein1958">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Finkelstein
 | first1 = David
 | title = Past-future asymmetry of the gravitational field of a point particle
 | journal = Physical Review
 | volume = 110
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 965–967
 | year = 1958
 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.110.965
 | bibcode = 1958PhRv..110..965F
}}</ref><ref name="Coecke2016">{{cite web
 |url = https://fqxi.org/community/forum/topic/2599
 |title = David Ritz Finkelstein (1929 - 2016)
 |author = Bob Coecke
 |date = 2016-02-16
 |website = FQXi BLOGS
 |publisher = The Foundational Questions Institute (FQXi)
 |access-date = 2022-03-11
}}</ref> In 1959, Finkelstein and [[Charles W. Misner]] found the gravitational kink, a [[topological defect]] in the gravitational metric, whose quantum theory could exhibit [[Spin (physics)|spin]]&nbsp;1/2.<ref name="Finkelstein1959">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Finkelstein
 | first1 = David
 | last2 = Misner
 | first2 = Charles W.
 | title = Some new conservation laws
 | journal = Annals of Physics
 | volume = 6
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 230–243
 | year = 1959
 | doi = 10.1016/0003-4916(59)90080-6
| bibcode = 1959AnPhy...6..230F
 }}</ref> The simplest kink exhibited an easily understood [[event horizon]] that led him to recognize the one in the [[Schwarzschild metric]] and eliminate its coordinate singularity.  In essence, Finkelstein determined that whatever falls past the [[Schwarzschild radius]] into a black hole cannot escape it; the membrane is one-directional. This important work influenced the decisions of [[Roger Penrose]] and [[John Archibald Wheeler]] to accept the physical existence of event horizons and black holes.<ref name="Overbye2008">{{cite web
 |url = https://www.nytimes.com/2008/04/14/science/14wheeler.html
 |title = John A. Wheeler, Physicist Who Coined the Term 'Black Hole,' Is Dead at 96
 |author = Overbye, Dennis
 |date = 2008
 |website = The New York Times
 |access-date = 2022-03-11
}}</ref>

Most of Finkelstein's work is directed toward a quantum theory of space-time structure. He early on accepted the conclusion of [[John von Neumann]] that anomalies of quantum mechanical measurement are anomalies of the logic of quantum mechanical systems. Therefore, he formed quantum analogues of set theory, the standard language for classical space-time structures, and proposed that space-time is a quantum set of space-time quanta dubbed "[[chronons]]", a form of [[quantum computer]] with [[Spin (physics)|spin]]s for quantum bits, as a quantum version of the cellular automaton of von Neumann. His early quantum space-times proving unphysical, he later studied chronons with a regularized form of [[Bose–Einstein statistics]] due to Tchavdar D. Palev.<ref name="Finkelstein2013">{{cite book
 | last1 = Finkelstein
 | first1 = David Ritz
 | year = 2013
 | chapter = Palev statistics and the chronon
 | editor-last1 = Dobrev
 | editor-first1 = Vladimir
 | title = Lie Theory and Its Applications in Physics
 | series = Springer Proceedings in Mathematics & Statistics
 | volume = 36
 | publisher = Springer
 | location = Tokyo
 | pages = 25–38
 | doi = 10.1007/978-4-431-54270-4_3
 | isbn = 978-4-431-54270-4
 | arxiv = 1201.1597
| s2cid = 58945899
 }}</ref>

He investigated [[ball lightning]] with Julio Rubinstein<ref name="Finkelstein1964">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Finkelstein
 | first1 = David
 | last2 = Rubinstein
 | first2 = Julio
 | title = Ball lightning
 | journal = Physical Review
 | volume = 135
 | issue = 2
 | pages = A390–A396
 | year = 1964
 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.135.A390
| bibcode = 1964PhRv..135..390F
 }}</ref> and [[James R. Powell (physicist)|James R. Powell]].<ref name="Finkelstein1970a">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Finkelstein
 | first1 = David
 | last2 = Powell
 | first2 = James R.
 | title = Earthquake lightning
 | journal = Nature
 | volume = 228
 | issue = 5273
 | pages = 759–760
 | year = 1970
 | doi = 10.1038/228759a0
| pmid = 16058686
 | bibcode = 1970Natur.228..759F
 | s2cid = 4248535
 }}</ref><ref name="Finkelstein1970b">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Finkelstein
 | first1 = David
 | last2 = Powell
 | first2 = James R.
 | title = Ball Lightning: Less well known than stroke lightning, ball lightning is about as frequent and can be simulated in the laboratory
 | journal = American Scientist
 | volume = 58
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 262–280
 | year = 1970
 | jstor = 27829081
}}</ref>
They concluded that ball lightning is most likely a wandering [[St. Elmo's fire]], a low-temperature [[soliton]] in the atmospheric electric current flow.

He also put forward an in-depth interpretation of the engraving ''[[Melencolia I]]'' of [[Albrecht Dürer]].<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last=Finkelstein |first=David Ritz |date=2006-02-27 |title=MELENCOLIA I: The physics of Albrecht Duerer |eprint=physics/0602185 |language=en}}</ref>

Finkelstein died from [[idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis]] in [[Atlanta]] on January 24, 2016, aged 86.<ref name="Cvitanovic2017"/><ref name="Bio"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/atlanta/obituary.aspx?pid=177436050|title=David Finkelstein Obituary - Atlanta, GA|work=Atlanta Journal-Constitution}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2016-01-25|title=Obituary: Physicist David Finkelstein, 86|url=https://atlantajewishtimes.timesofisrael.com/obituary-david-finkelstein-86/|access-date=2021-04-12|website=Atlanta Jewish Times|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Universal relativity ==
Influenced by his discussions of [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] [[philosophy]] at the [[Mind and Life Institute|Mind and Life dialogues]], Finkelstein developed a philosophical theory of "universal relativity" which he thought might help advance physics. According to Finkelstein:<ref name="Finkelstein2003">{{cite book
 | last1 = Finkelstein
 | first1 = David
 | year = 2003
 | chapter = Emptiness and relativity
 | editor-last1 = Wallace
 | editor-first1 = B. Alan
 | title = Buddhism and Science: Breaking New Ground
 | publisher = Columbia University Press
 | location = New York
 | pages = 365–386
 | chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=10ysAgAAQBAJ&pg=365
 | oclc = 756510558
 | isbn = 978-0-231-12335-8
 | s2cid = 14908829
 | citeseerx = 10.1.1.68.4935
}}</ref>
<blockquote>The Buddhist principle that all is [[Śūnyatā|empty]] is understood by some as the principle that all is relative ([[Robert Thurman|Thurman]] 1993). This universal relativity principle is more embracing though less structured than Einstein's [[General relativity|general relativity principle]], which still admits many absolutes. The major changes in physics in this century have been extensions of relativity at one level or another, and I think a further extension is due, at an even deeper level of physics than the previous. Philosophical inquiry has aided such extensions before, and it could do so again. A philosophical argument for a universal relativity could be a useful guide for future physics.</blockquote>
